The morning light hit the kitchen counter at 6:47, same angle as yesterday, same dust motes performing their slow ballet through the beam. I stood there waiting for the coffee maker to finish its gurgling confession, thinking about how repetition wears grooves in the mind until what was once remarkable becomes invisible.

My grandmother kept a diary for sixty-three years. Not the reflective kind—no weather reports of the soul. Just facts. "Planted tomatoes. Rain at four. Mr. Henderson's dog in the azaleas again." I found them in a cedar chest after she died, thirty-four volumes, each day accounted for like a ledger entry in some cosmic bookkeeping. At first I felt sad for her, all that observation without interpretation. Then I noticed something. On March 14, 1987, she wrote "First robin" with an exclamation point. She never used exclamation points. That robin mattered. The restraint made it louder.

We live in an age of exclamation point inflation. Everything is amazing, devastating, unmissable. The algorithm feeds us peaks without valleys, and we wonder why we feel numb at the summit. I deleted my social media accounts in 2019, not as a statement but as an experiment. The first month felt like phantom limb syndrome, reaching for a phone that no longer held anything I wanted. By the third month, I started noticing the particular green of the maple outside my window, how it shifted from emerald to something almost black as summer deepened. I'd seen that tree for six years. Never really looked.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called *wabi-sabi*: the beauty of impermanence, imperfection, incompleteness. A cracked teacup repaired with gold. A garden designed to look untended. We resist it, we Americans, with our self-improvement protocols and our pursuit of closure. We want the healed wound, not the scar. But the scar is where the interesting texture lives.

I met a woman in a used bookstore in Portland who had spent thirty years collecting rejection letters. She kept them in chronological order, three-ring binders, literary magazines and agents and publishers who passed on her novels. "The first one I cried over," she told me, running her finger down a column of names. "The fiftieth one I framed." She sold her fourth novel at sixty-one. It was about a woman who collects rejection letters. She told me the binders were her real life's work, the novels just footnotes.

We misunderstand failure. We treat it as deviation from path instead of path itself. Every successful person I've ever interviewed—and I've interviewed hundreds for magazine profiles—has a private archive of almosts and not-quites they rarely mention in the polished version. The tech founder who went bankrupt twice. The surgeon who failed her boards. The poet who didn't publish for twenty years. These aren't digressions. They're the compost everything grew from.

Memory is another liar. I remember my childhood as mostly golden, but when I found an old journal from age thirteen, I was shocked by the despair. "Everything is gray," I wrote. "I will never be happy." I don't remember that boy. He got edited out in the revision process, replaced by a nostalgic fiction that serves the present better. We're all unreliable narrators of our own lives, and that's not necessarily a flaw. The edited version might be the true one, in the way a novel is truer than a transcript.

I think about time differently as I get older. Not as sand through an hourglass—that's too passive—but as something I sculpt. Some hours I make rough and utilitarian, others I sand to smoothness. The pandemic years were strange clay. I learned to bake bread, like everyone else. I also learned that I could go three days without speaking aloud and not feel lonely. That worried me at first. Now I think it was just another way of being human, one our culture doesn't have much room for.

The last time I visited my hometown, I drove past the house where I grew up. Someone had painted it gray; it had been white. The oak tree I'd climbed was gone, probably a casualty of age or storm. I felt nothing, which felt like a betrayal of something. Shouldn't there be emotion? A swelling of soundtrack? Instead I just noted the change, like my grandmother with her tomatoes. "House is gray now. Tree removed." Maybe that's enough. Maybe the feeling comes later, in dreams, in the way certain smells still trigger something I can't name.

I've been reading about deep time. Geologists think in millions of years. The Appalachian Mountains were once as tall as the Himalayas; now they're hills, and in another hundred million years they'll be plains. Nothing we build will last. Nothing we destroy is permanent. The plastic in the oceans will eventually subduct into the mantle and be reborn as something else. This isn't comfort exactly, but it's perspective. Our urgency is real and also temporary.

I used to want to change the world. Now I want to change the room I'm in, and trust the ripple. I volunteer at a literacy center, teaching adults to read. Maria is sixty-four, came from Guatemala, works nights cleaning offices. She can read a children's book now, slowly, her finger tracing each word. The pride on her face when she finished *The Very Hungry Caterpillar*—I keep that image like a stone in my pocket, something to hold when the news gets too loud.

The news is always too loud now. We're not built for this much information, this much suffering rendered in high definition. I don't know the solution. I know that I limit my intake, that I donate to causes instead of just feeling bad, that I try to be present with the person in front of me. These are small strategies against a large problem. They don't scale. Maybe scaling isn't the point.

There's a bird that nests on the ledge outside my office window. I don't know what kind. Small, brown, unremarkable. Every spring she builds her nest in the same spot, raises her chicks, teaches them to fly. They leave. She leaves. The nest stays through winter, slowly falling apart, until she returns to build again. I watch this cycle without knowing what it means. Maybe it means persistence. Maybe it means nothing, just the bird doing what birds do. The not-knowing is its own kind of peace.

I used to need everything to mean something. Now I find meaning in the search for meaning, in the questions that stay open like doors. A friend asked me recently what I believe in. I said I believe in the conversation we're having, in the coffee growing cold, in the particular slant of light that will be different in ten minutes and gone in an hour. I believe in the temporary, which is another word for the real.

The coffee maker finished. I poured, I sat, I watched the dust motes until they disappeared into the general brightness of the day beginning. Nothing special happened. Nothing special needed to.
